abstract: This paper argues that survey researchers routinely fail to provide evidence that respondents interpret questions as intended, undermining the validity of survey-based inference. The authors call for explicit tests of question comprehension and propose approaches to gather such evidence. They frame this as a foundational methodological gap in survey research practice.
key_claims: Survey research generally lacks empirical evidence that respondents understand questions in the way researchers intend.
Without such evidence, inferences drawn from survey responses rest on unverified assumptions about shared meaning.
Researchers should systematically test and document respondent comprehension as part of standard survey methodology.
methods: Methodological critique and prescriptive argument regarding survey research practice.
(From abstract only) Discussion of approaches for eliciting and evaluating evidence of respondent comprehension.
findings: The abstract does not report specific empirical findings; the central observation is that evidence of comprehension is largely absent from published survey work.
contributions: Foregrounds respondent comprehension as an underexamined validity threat in survey research.
Advocates a shift in norms toward providing explicit evidence that questions are understood as intended.
Sets an agenda for developing and adopting tools to test question interpretation.
framing: The paper positions itself within survey methodology and measurement validity debates, extending long-standing concerns about question wording and cognitive interviewing into a broader claim about evidentiary standards. It speaks to political science and social science audiences that rely heavily on survey data for causal and descriptive inference.
